## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Makasajātaka* (Ja 44), translated in English as *The Mosquito*, is a short narrative included in the Jātaka collection of the Khuddaka Nikāya [SuttaCentral]. According to the commentary's frame narrative (*paccuppannavatthu*), the Buddha recounted the tale while traveling on an alms-pilgrimage from Sāvatthī through the Magadha country, occasioned by the foolish villagers of a certain hamlet [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877; Readings from the Jatakas]. These villagers, constantly harassed by mosquito bites while working in the woods, banded together with weapons to attack the insects, only to wound and strike each other instead [Fausböll 1877].
To illustrate the folly of lacking sense, the story of the past (*atītavatthu*) recounts how a son attempted to kill a mosquito that had landed on his father's bald head; swinging an axe, he struck and killed both the mosquito and his father with a single blow [Anandajoti 2010]. The core moral is summarized in verse 168 (*Seyyo amitto matiyā upeto...*), which praises an intelligent enemy over a foolish friend who brings destruction through sheer thoughtlessness [Anandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1877]. At the conclusion of the story (*samodhāna*), the Bodhisatta is identified as the wise traveling merchant (*paṇḍitavāṇijo*) who witnessed the event and uttered the verse [Fausböll 1877].
